This research looked at two medicines used to treat a condition called Relapsing-Remitting Multiple Sclerosis (RRMS): alemtuzumab and interferon beta-1a. Three studies were done with 1694 people each. They compared how well these medicines worked over 24 to 36 months.

Alemtuzumab, given at a lower dose of 12 mg every day, seemed to help less often with something called "relapses" (when symptoms get worse suddenly), and it might also help with getting worse disability. It didn't seem to make much difference in how many "T2 lesions" showed up on MRI scans, which are spots seen on brain scans that can mean MS activity. Over time, the medicine didn't seem to change how well people could move around (measured by something called the Expanded Disability Status Scale).

For alemtuzumab given at a higher dose of 24 mg every day, it seemed to help even more with relapses and disability worsening. But the results for this higher dose weren't as clear because there wasn't enough information.

Both medicines caused some side effects like feeling sick or having infections, but the chance of serious problems was about the same for both. The medicine alemtuzumab needs careful watching because it can cause serious health issues, so doctors need to keep an eye out for them.

Overall, alemtuzumab seems to work better than interferon beta-1a at reducing relapses and disability worsening, especially with the higher dose. But the evidence isn't perfect, so we're not sure about all the details.

This study looked at a new treatment for something called Lichen Migrans, which is a skin condition. They found only one study that was big enough to be useful. In this study, they gave two different treatments to people with Lichen Migrans: one group got a cream called imiquimod and another cream called tazarotene, both applied twice a week for three months. After stopping the creams, they removed the spots and checked if they were gone completely. 

The study found that about half of the people in each group had their spots go away completely. But the difference wasn't strong enough to say for sure that one treatment worked better than the other. 

They also noticed that the group using both creams had more redness in their skin after treatment. However, some people dropped out of the study because the creams made their skin too red, especially those using both creams together.

The study didn't tell us much about the creams' side effects. Overall, there isn't a lot of good information about treating Lichen Migrans. For some people, doctors might try removing the spots surgically, but this isn't always possible. For others, they might use creams like imiquimod or 5-fluorouracil. Sometimes, adding tazarotene to imiquimod can make the skin more red, so it's important to talk to a doctor about the best treatment. More studies are needed to learn more about these treatments.

This review looked at six studies with a total of 885 patients to see if adding a special kind of cuff to a prosthetic graft helps keep blood flowing better after surgery. Two studies compared grafts with and without a cuff for below the knee bypass surgeries. One study found that the group with the cuff had slightly better blood flow at 12 and 24 months, but not at 3 years. Another study didn't find a difference between the two groups at 3 years. 

One study compared pre-filled grafts with those filled later. It didn't find a difference in how well the grafts worked. Another study compared grafts made by sewing veins together with those that had a cuff. The sewn grafts had better blood flow at 24 months, but this didn't help save more legs. 

Overall, there's some evidence that adding a cuff to a prosthetic graft might help keep blood flowing better for below the knee bypasses, but it doesn't seem to help save more legs. The evidence isn't very strong because most of the studies weren't big enough. Grafts that are pre-filled work about the same as those with a cuff. Using veins that have been sewn together might help keep blood flowing better, but it doesn't seem to help save more legs. More research is needed, especially focusing on below the knee vein cuff prosthetic grafts.

This review looked at studies about medicines and talk therapy to help people who have a condition called Post-Divorce Depression (PDD) feel better and stay that way. We checked 10 studies with 840 people to see if the medicine or talk therapy worked. Most of the studies had good methods, but some had problems like people knowing which group they were in or who paid for the study.

For the medicine part, four out of five studies said that people who took the medicine were less likely to get worse feelings than those who took a sugar pill. But we're not sure because the studies weren't perfect. About one-third of people dropped out of the studies, so we don’t know if the medicine made them leave or not.

For the talk therapy part, there wasn't enough information to say if it helped. One study said that continuing talk therapy might be helpful, but we can't be very sure because there weren't many people in the study.

The studies didn't compare medicines to talking therapies or to usual care. Also, the studies didn't look at how well people felt overall or if the medicines caused any bad side effects.

Overall, we don't have strong proof that medicines or talk therapy helps prevent people with PDD from getting worse. More studies are needed to find out if these treatments work and if they cause any problems. It's also important to look at how well people feel after using these treatments.

This research looked at seven studies with 345 people to see if starting food sooner or later helps sick people get better faster. They looked at things like how long people stayed in the hospital, if they got infections, and if they needed extra help breathing. But the studies had some problems, so we can't be sure about their results. 

For how soon to start food, five studies showed that starting sooner didn't seem to make a big difference in how long people lived. Four studies didn't tell us when exactly, but they also didn't show a clear difference. Some studies said people who started eating sooner had a little bit longer stays in the hospital, but this wasn't always true. No studies showed a clear difference in getting infections or needing help with breathing.

For people who needed extra help with eating, one study showed that starting sooner didn't seem to cause more problems with their stomach or intestines. But again, the studies weren't perfect, so we're not sure about this either.

One study compared starting food sooner with giving extra medicine through a vein. This study also didn't show a clear difference in how long people lived, if they got infections, or if they needed extra help breathing.

Overall, the studies aren't strong enough to give us a clear answer. We need more research with bigger groups of people to know if starting food sooner really helps sick people.

output: This research looked at seven studies involving 1839 people who had blood clots and were being treated differently. Most of the studies had some problems, like not treating everyone equally or mixing up where the treatment happened. The studies found that people who got treated at home with a medicine called LMWH had fewer blood clots come back compared to those who got treated in a hospital with another medicine called UFH. There wasn't much difference in things like big or small injuries or death. Some people said they felt better when they were treated at home. But the studies didn't look at whether home treatment was cheaper or if it worked better overall. Since most hospitals are starting to treat people at home with this medicine, it seems likely that home treatment will become the usual way to do it. Now, doctors need to figure out how to make sure home treatment works well and safely for everyone.

This research looked at two studies to see if a program could help people check their skin more carefully for signs of a serious skin problem called melanoma. In one study, 1356 people got special instructions and videos about checking their skin, while another group got different advice about eating healthy. The study didn't find out if this helped prevent melanoma deaths or if it led to more unnecessary tests. 

In the other study, 63,035 adults in Australia had some education about skin checks and free screenings. But they didn't follow up with any new information about whether this helped or hurt. Another study that would have compared screened people to those who weren't screened was never done because of money problems. 

The studies weren't perfect; it's hard to know if the people knew they were being watched or if the doctors knew who was being checked. Also, we don't have enough information to say if checking skin helps or hurts. Right now, there isn't enough good evidence to decide if checking skin should be done as part of regular health check-ups. More research is needed to find out if checking skin can help prevent melanoma deaths and if it causes more tests than necessary.

A study looked at a treatment called pembrolizumab for people with a type of cancer called advanced urothelial carcinoma. This cancer comes back after other treatments. The study compared using just pembrolizumab to using chemotherapy, which is another type of treatment.

The study found that people who got pembrolizumab might live longer than those who got chemotherapy. They might also feel better and have fewer serious side effects from the treatment. However, we're not very sure about these findings because the study was small and some parts weren't clear.

Pembrolizumab might help people get better faster, but it doesn't seem to affect how often they stop treatment because of side effects. Also, the study shows that fewer people in the pembrolizumab group died over a year, but this could be because the chemotherapy group had more people die.

Overall, the study suggests that pembrolizumab might be better than chemotherapy for treating this type of cancer, but we need more information to be really sure. The study was paid for by the company that makes pembrolizumab, so there might be reasons why it's positive about the drug.

output: This review looked at three studies to see if a medicine called aripiprazole helps kids and teenagers with autism behave better. The studies were mostly done with children and young people. Most of these studies were done well, but one had some missing information. The main finding was that kids and teens who took aripiprazole had fewer problems like being too irritable, being hyperactive, and doing repetitive actions compared to those who took a sugar pill. But they also gained more weight and had more trouble sleeping and shaking their hands. One study found that when kids stopped taking the medicine, about half of them had their old problems come back. This suggests that it might be good to check again after a while to see if the medicine still works. The studies were partly paid for by companies that make the medicine. The rules for diagnosing autism changed a bit since these studies were done, so the results might not apply to everyone now.

This review looked at different types of solutions used during a treatment called peritoneal dialysis (PD) for people who need it. They checked if using solutions with lower sugar levels and a more neutral pH helped keep their kidneys working better and made less waste build up in their bodies. They also saw if using a special sugar called icodextrin had any benefits.

The review found that using solutions with lower sugar levels and a more neutral pH helped keep the kidneys working better and made less waste build up over time. This happened in most of the studies they looked at, but the evidence wasn't very strong because some of the studies weren't done very well.

Using icodextrin, a special sugar, seemed to help keep the body from getting too full with fluid and could help remove more waste from the body. But the evidence for this wasn't very strong either, and we don't know if it helps prevent infections or other problems.

Overall, the review suggests that using solutions with lower sugar levels and a more neutral pH might help keep the kidneys working better and reduce waste in the body. However, we still need more good studies to be sure about the exact benefits and risks of these solutions.

This study looked at whether doctors could do better at putting in tubes called lines into patients using something called two-dimensional ultrasound instead of just looking at where the tube should go. They checked 35 studies with 5,108 people to see if ultrasound helped. Most of the studies weren't very good, but some parts showed ultrasound worked well. 

Using ultrasound made it much less likely that doctors would accidentally put the tube into a blood vessel. It also made it easier to put the tube in the first time, which means fewer tries were needed. Ultrasound also helped reduce the chance of a small collection of blood forming around the tube. 

Overall, using ultrasound seemed to make things safer and better. But there wasn't enough information to know if it worked better for doctors who have more experience or for patients who might be more likely to have problems. Also, the studies didn't tell us if ultrasound was better than another type of ultrasound called Doppler. So while ultrasound seems helpful, we need more research to be sure.

output: This study looked at seven clinical trials involving 538 people over 18 years old who had a type of liver disease called chronic hepatitis C. They compared a medicine called nitazoxanide to a sugar pill or nothing at all. Six out of the seven trials also gave other medicines to everyone. One trial found that people taking nitazoxanide didn't die more often than those taking a sugar pill or nothing. Nitazoxanide didn't seem to cause more side effects than the sugar pill or nothing. It seemed to help people get rid of the virus better than the sugar pill or nothing did. But it wasn't clear if this happened because of the nitazoxanide or just because the trials weren't perfect. There was also some uncertainty about whether nitazoxanide helped people feel better after treatment. Nitazoxanide didn't seem to make people's blood tests show they were getting better faster either. The study couldn't tell if nitazoxanide helped people feel better overall or if it made their livers healthier. The studies weren't very good, so we can't be sure about these results. We don't know if nitazoxanide helps people with other types of hepatitis C. More good studies are needed to find out.

This research looked at hormone replacement therapy (HRT) for women who had surgery for ovarian cancer. They found information from three studies that involved 350 women. These studies looked at women who had different stages of ovarian cancer and some had gone through menopause while others hadn't yet. The studies compared women who took HRT with those who didn't.

The studies found that HRT might help women live longer, but it's not clear if it makes their lives better or worse. It also seems like HRT might not affect the chance of getting breast cancer, but there wasn't enough information to know for sure. HRT might not help prevent strokes or heart attacks, but again, we're not sure because there wasn't much data.

The studies weren't perfect, so we can't be completely certain about these findings. More research is needed to learn more about HRT for women who have ovarian cancer. While HRT might help some women live longer, we don't know if it causes harm. More studies are needed to give us a clearer picture.

output: This study looked at a medicine called TXA to help stop bleeding after a woman gives birth. They studied 20,412 women who had bleeding right after their baby was born. Two big studies showed that giving TXA through a needle in the arm helped keep women alive less often than just regular care. The medicine seemed to work best if it was given within one to three hours after the baby was born. It didn't seem to help prevent serious sickness or needing blood transfusions. But it did make it easier to close up the cut where the baby came out and made it less likely that a woman would need surgery to stop the bleeding. Giving TXA through a vein seems to be helpful, but sometimes hospitals don't have the equipment to do that. So doctors need to find ways to give it that don't require a hospital setting.

This research looked at different ways to transfer embryos during in-vitro fertilization (IVF) to see which might help more women have babies. They studied 2165 women who had IVF. Some studies compared transferring one embryo at a time (single cycle) versus transferring two or more embryos at once (double cycle). Other studies looked at transferring embryos in stages called cleavage-stage or blastocyst-stage.

The studies found that having two or more cycles of transferring one embryo at a time (repeated single cycle) didn't seem to help women have more babies overall. But it did lower the chances of having twins or triplets, which is good. 

When looking at just the first cycle, transferring two embryos at once (double cycle) seemed to help more women have babies, but it also meant there was a higher chance of twins or triplets. 

Overall, the research suggests that having one cycle of transferring one embryo at a time might be better for most women. It helps fewer women have twins or triplets, but it also means fewer women end up with a baby. More research is needed to know if this works best for all types of women.

In a study looking at a special kind of fish oil called marine-derived n-3 PUFAs, researchers looked at how it affects people who had a stroke. They studied 29 different studies, but only nine gave information about how well the treatment worked. Most of these studies were done fairly well, but some smaller ones weren't as good.

The study found that within the first few months after having a stroke, this special fish oil didn't seem to help with how well someone could do everyday tasks or their mood. It also didn't seem to affect the chances of having another stroke or improving overall quality of life. However, it did show that people taking the fish oil didn't have more bleeding problems compared to those not taking it.

For longer follow-ups (after more than three months), the study found that the fish oil might help a little bit with how well people can move around and do daily activities. But again, the evidence wasn't strong enough to be sure.

Overall, the study isn't very confident about whether this fish oil helps after a stroke because there just isn't enough good-quality information. Doctors think we need more studies to know if it's helpful and safe. They also suggest that doctors start giving this treatment as soon as possible after a stroke happens and use clear tests to measure how well people are doing. More research is needed to figure out the best dose and how to give it.

This study looked at different medicines called sulfonylureas and meglitinides to see if they help prevent a condition called type 2 diabetes. They studied 10,000 people who had some risk of getting type 2 diabetes. Some people got one of these medicines by themselves, while others got a sugar pill or other treatments. The study lasted from 6 months to 5 years.

The medicines didn't seem to lower the chance of getting type 2 diabetes. But when they looked closely at just one medicine called nateglinide, it seemed to slightly lower the chance of dying from any cause. However, this finding wasn't very strong because there weren't many people in the study.

For people taking nateglinide, about 6 out of every 100 died compared to about 6 out of every 100 in the group that took a sugar pill. This difference wasn't big enough to be sure it wasn't just chance.

The medicines also didn't seem to lower the chances of having serious problems like heart attacks, strokes, or needing to go to the hospital for heart trouble. But again, the study wasn't large enough to be very confident about this.

Overall, the study found that these medicines didn't seem to help prevent type 2 diabetes or its complications. The evidence isn't strong enough to say for sure if they work or not. Most of the studies didn't look at important things like how well people felt or how much money their health care cost.

This review looked at 21 studies to see if certain roads and bike paths help keep cyclists safer. Most of these studies used before-and-after comparisons, which means they looked at what happened before and after changes were made to the roads. None of the studies found that adding special bike lanes called cycle lanes really helped prevent bike accidents. 

When comparing bike paths and regular roads, the studies didn't find a clear difference in how often bikes got into accidents. But some studies suggested that redesigning parts of bike paths that have lots of cars might actually make it more dangerous for cyclists. 

Using slower speeds in cities seemed to help keep cyclists safer. Changing some intersections to roundabouts, which are like circles where cars go around, could make things worse for cyclists. Adding bike lanes right at the corners of streets could also make things worse.

The studies also found that putting bike paths next to busy streets or adding bike lanes that cross over small roads could make it more dangerous for cyclists. But it wasn't clear if having bike paths or stopping lines near the start of bike rides helped or hurt safety.

Overall, the studies had some problems, like not always comparing the same types of roads before and after changes, and not always looking at all the different ways people ride bikes. Because of these issues, we can't be sure if making roads better for bikes really helps keep people safe. More studies need to be done to figure this out.

This review looked at 71 studies comparing different medicines used to treat mental illness: chlorpromazine, olanzapine, risperidone, and quetiapine. The studies didn't look at how much these medicines cost. 

For short-term treatment, it seemed like olanzapine worked better than chlorpromazine. People taking olanzapine had more improvement in their condition, but there wasn't a big difference in how well they did over time. Chlorpromazine caused more side effects called extrapyramidal symptoms, which made people feel worse. Olanzapine also seemed to make people feel better about their overall health.

Risperidone and chlorpromazine didn't seem to work differently. They both helped people feel better, but risperidone seemed to improve quality of life more. Chlorpromazine caused more side effects, but the studies weren't sure if this was true because the evidence wasn't strong.

Quetiapine didn't seem to work better than chlorpromazine. It also caused fewer side effects, but people taking quetiapine felt better about their health. Most of the studies included people who were in hospitals in China, so the results might not apply to everyone else. The studies mostly looked at short-term treatment, so we don't know how well these medicines work over longer periods. The studies showed that chlorpromazine caused more side effects, but the evidence wasn't very strong.

This study looked at whether taking calcium before and during pregnancy helps prevent some problems. They studied 1355 women in different countries like Argentina, South Africa, and Zimbabwe. Most of the women were those who had already become pregnant or were close to 20 weeks along. The study wasn't perfect because many women dropped out before the end. Some women got calcium every day, while others got a sugar pill.

The study found that starting calcium before pregnancy didn’t seem to lower the chance of having pre-eclampsia, which is a serious condition during pregnancy. However, it might slightly lower the chance of losing the baby or having a stillborn baby, but the results weren’t very clear. Calcium didn’t seem to affect other problems like needing a cesarean section, being born too early, or having a low birth weight baby.

For most other things like birth weight, preterm birth, or getting sick after the baby is born, calcium didn’t seem to make much difference. The study couldn’t tell if calcium helped prevent some specific problems like perinatal death or needing special care in the hospital.

Overall, the study suggests that starting calcium before or during pregnancy might help a little bit, but the results aren’t strong enough to know for sure. More research is needed to see if calcium really does help prevent these problems. Also, we don’t know if it’s easy for women to take calcium supplements before and during pregnancy.

output: This study looked at ways to help people who smoke cut down or stop smoking. They tried different methods like using special medicines called NRT, which helps with nicotine, and other things like e-cigarettes. But none of these methods were tested to see if they really help people stay healthy while still smoking. Most of the studies looked at NRT, which is a medicine that comes in different forms like gum or spray. When people used NRT, they were more likely to cut down on the number of cigarettes they smoke or even quit completely. However, the evidence isn't very strong because many of the studies had some problems that might affect the results. For example, some people knew they were getting the medicine, which could have changed how they acted. Also, there weren't enough studies to know if other things like e-cigarettes or special advice really work. So, while NRT seems to help, we don't have enough good information to say for sure if other methods work. More studies need to be done to find out. For now, people who want to quit can try NRT, but we're not sure if other methods will work as well.

This study looked at five trials involving 297 women who had a type of abnormal skin growth called high-grade VIN. The trials tested different treatments to see if they worked better than a placebo, which is like a pretend treatment. 

Three out of the five trials were considered to have strong evidence, meaning the results are very reliable. These trials showed that a cream called imiquimod helped more women get better from their condition compared to a placebo. At first, 58 out of 62 women who used the imiquimod cream got better, while only 0 out of 42 women who used the placebo cream got better. This difference was very clear and lasted for up to six months. After one year, about 38 out of 24 women who used the imiquimod cream got better, compared to 0 out of 23 women who used the placebo. But some women had to use less of the cream because it made their skin red, sore, or itchy.

One trial also looked at another cream called cidofovir. It didn't seem to work much better than imiquimod after six months. Some women had more side effects from the imiquimod cream, but these were mostly mild.

There wasn't enough information to know if the creams would help prevent the growth from turning into something more serious. More studies are being done to find out.

So, imiquimod seems to be a good treatment for high-grade VIN, but we need more long-term information to be sure. Cidofovir might be a good choice too, but we need more studies to compare them properly.

Nineteen studies with 1870 women were reviewed. The studies showed that using misoprostol made the cervix open better than not using anything, and this helped fewer women need their cervix opened with tools during the procedure. It also seemed to help prevent some problems during the procedure, like tears in the cervix or going into the wrong place inside the uterus. But using misoprostol also caused more discomfort, like mild belly pain and bleeding.

The researchers think misoprostol is a good choice because it helps the cervix open better and causes fewer problems, but it also causes more discomfort. More research is needed to know if the benefits of misoprostol outweigh the extra discomfort.

This study looked at different medicines used to treat a type of infection called chlamydia trachomatis (CT). They studied 2715 people, mostly men, who had this infection. Some took a medicine called azithromycin, while others took doxycycline or ofloxacin. 

For men, taking azithromycin didn't seem to help stop the infection better than doxycycline. But it wasn't clear if it helped more or less. Also, men who took azithromycin seemed to have fewer side effects, like stomach problems, compared to those who took doxycycline. 

For women, the study wasn't sure if azithromycin worked better or worse than doxycycline. There weren't many studies about women, so we don't know much about them. 

The study also wasn't sure if doxycycline worked better than another medicine called ofloxacin. And it wasn't sure if either of these medicines worked better or worse than ofloxacin for women. 

The study found that for men, using azithromycin might not be as good as using doxycycline to stop the infection. But for women, it's not clear if azithromycin works better or worse. 

Because women often have infections that don't cause symptoms, it's important to do more studies to see how well these medicines work for women. These studies should include more women and look at things like how well the medicines work, if they cause side effects, and if the infections come back after treatment. It would also be helpful to look at how well people take their medicine and if the infections become resistant to the medicines.

output: A study looked at 752 new mothers who had a tear in their vagina during childbirth. Some of these women got a special test called EAUS right away, while others just had the usual care. The study found that women who got the EAUS test had fewer cases of a serious problem where they couldn't control their bowels for more than six months after giving birth. But, they also had more pain in the area around the bottom for about three months after the birth. The study didn't find much difference in other problems like leaking stool or gas, or in how happy the women felt overall. The study only looked at women who had given birth for the first time. While the results are promising, they come from just one study, so we need more research to be sure. More studies are needed to see if this test helps prevent problems later and to make sure it doesn't cause too much pain. Also, we need to know if the cost of doing this test is worth it and if it makes women feel better. Future studies might look at whether the test works better in women who have given birth before.

In a review of 14 studies with 978 children who had kidney stones, researchers looked at different ways to remove the stones. They found that for some methods, like using sound waves to break up the stones (called shock wave lithotripsy), they weren't sure if it worked better than other methods. For example, when comparing shock wave lithotripsy to another method called dissolution therapy, they weren't sure if shock wave lithotripsy was better at getting rid of the stones or if it caused more problems. 

For other methods, like using a tiny camera to look inside the kidney (ureteroscopy) or a special tool to break up the stones (mini-percutaneous nephrolithotripsy), they also weren't sure if these methods were better. One study showed that shock wave lithotripsy might have a slightly lower chance of getting rid of the stones completely, but it could also mean fewer serious problems during treatment. However, there were more times when people needed extra procedures to fix the problem.

The review also looked at whether using medicine to relax muscles (alpha-blockers) helped get rid of stones. They found that these medicines might help more stones come out, but they weren't sure if they caused more problems. They weren't sure about whether these medicines caused serious side effects or if they led to more extra procedures.

Overall, the evidence wasn't strong enough to give clear answers about which treatments work best. This means doctors and parents need to be cautious and consider many factors when deciding on a treatment plan. More studies are needed to provide clearer information for children with kidney stones.

This research looked at 10 studies with 697 children who received treatment for their health problems through the internet. Some of the children had headaches, others had other issues like arthritis or sickle cell disease. The studies also included children with different types of long-term pain. The average age of the children was around 13 years old.

The researchers thought they did a good job picking the studies and making sure everyone followed through with them. But they weren't completely sure if some things might have affected the results. They looked at 16 different ways the studies could have been done, but could only do 13 of those.

For children with headaches, the studies showed that after getting the treatment, their headaches were less severe. This happened in 7 out of 8 studies with 379 children. But it didn't work as well when they checked again later. The studies also didn't show that the treatments helped with other problems like feeling sad or worried.

For children with different types of long-term pain, the studies didn't find that the internet-based treatments helped reduce pain or make people feel better. Sometimes the treatments seemed to help a little bit, but the studies weren't big enough to be sure.

Overall, the researchers think the treatments might help, but they're not very confident about it. They believe there's a small chance that the treatments might actually help, but they're not sure. More studies are needed to learn more about this.

This study looked at a group of 1956 adults with HIV who hadn't taken a medicine called abacavir before. They wanted to see if checking their bodies for something called HLA-B*57:01 could help prevent a bad reaction to abacavir. The study divided people into two groups - one where they checked for HLA-B*57:01 before taking abacavir, and another where they didn't check but still took the medicine. 

The group that checked for HLA-B*57:01 had fewer people having a very bad reaction to abacavir compared to those who didn't check. About 1650 people in the screening group had a reaction, while about 1644 people in the other group had a reaction. This means the screening group had about half as many reactions. The researchers think this might be because the screening helps doctors avoid giving abacavir to people who might have a bad reaction.

However, the study wasn't perfect. It might have missed some people who had reactions because they weren't followed up on. Also, the doctors who decided if someone had a bad reaction might have been influenced by seeing more people in the screening group. Despite these small problems, the study suggests that checking for HLA-B*57:01 before giving abacavir might help prevent a bad reaction.

But remember, this study only looked at one type of reaction to one medicine. More studies are needed to know if this works for other medicines and in different groups of people.

output: This study looked at different ways to treat a condition called stress urinary incontinence, which makes it hard to control when you need to go to the bathroom. They studied 5417 women who had this problem. The study found that a surgery called open retropubic colposuspension worked well. It helped about 68.9% to 88.0% of women stop leaking urine. This surgery seemed to work better than other treatments like just waiting or taking medicine. Over time, more women stayed dry after this surgery compared to other surgeries. However, newer surgeries called TVT and laparoscopic colposuspension might be cheaper in the long run, but we don't know if they're as good as open retropubic colposuspension yet. These newer surgeries might cause some problems like needing a catheter or having trouble going to the bathroom, but they might be easier to recover from. Open retropubic colposuspension has a chance of making your bladder fall down, but it's less likely to cause problems with peeing. Laparoscopic colposuspension might be quicker to heal from, but we need more information on how well it works in the long term.

This research looked at seven studies involving 1074 children and teenagers aged 2 to 18 who had a long-term joint pain condition. The studies compared different types of medicines called NSAIDs with other medicines. However, none of the studies compared the same NSAID against another NSAID. Because the studies weren't perfect, it's hard to know if the medicines worked better than each other. 

The studies didn't find strong proof that one NSAID was better than another for reducing pain. They did find that some medicines like ibuprofen and aspirin helped reduce pain, but the studies weren't large enough to be sure. One study showed that taking a lower dose of meloxicam might work as well as a higher dose. Another study found that people who took ibuprofen or aspirin felt much better after using the medicine.

The studies also found that some children experienced side effects from the medicines, but not many. The most common side effect was feeling sick or having a stomach ache. Some children stopped taking the medicine because they got sick from it, but again, this wasn't very common.

Because the studies weren't perfect and there wasn't enough information, we can't say for sure if these medicines help or hurt children with joint pain. We also don't have enough information to know about other things like how well the children can move their joints or how their overall health is affected. More studies would be needed to answer those questions.

output:
This research looked at different treatments for a condition called xerostomia, which is when you feel very dry in your mouth after having radiation therapy for cancer. They studied 3520 people who had received radiation therapy to their head and neck area. They found that a medicine called amifostine might help prevent the feeling of dry mouth right after radiation therapy and up to three months later. This helps more than half of the people who take it compared to those who don't take it. Amifostine also seems to make more saliva come out of the mouth for up to 12 months after radiation therapy. However, we're not sure if this effect lasts longer than 12 months.

Amifostine also makes people feel sick more often, have lower blood pressure, and have more allergic reactions. But it doesn't seem to affect how long people live or how well they feel overall.

There's not enough good evidence to know if another medicine called pilocarpine works better or worse. Pilocarpine might make people sweat more though.

The research also found that amifostine might cause more vomiting, nausea, and allergic reactions. Other medicines like palifermin didn't seem to work better or worse than a placebo.

Overall, amifostine might help with dry mouth, but it costs a lot and has some side effects. It's important to weigh these benefits against the costs and risks. There isn't strong evidence that any other medicine works better.

This research looked at five new studies, making a total of twelve studies that included 2300 people with mouth cancer. Most of these studies had some problems that might affect how reliable their results are. The studies didn't compare different types of surgery for removing the main tumor. They mostly compared two ways of doing neck surgery - one right away (elective) and the other after waiting a bit (therapeutic).

The studies that compared doing neck surgery right away versus waiting to do it later found that neither way seemed better at keeping the cancer from coming back or helping people live longer. But one study found that doing neck surgery right away might help keep the cancer from coming back a little bit more than waiting.

Some studies looked at whether doing more or less neck surgery helps. They couldn't really tell which way was better. One study found that doing more neck surgery might help keep the cancer from coming back, but another study said it didn't make a difference.

There were also studies looking at whether doing surgery with radiation works better than just radiation. The results weren't clear, and some of the studies had problems that made it hard to trust the results.

Overall, the studies didn't give us much information to decide which way of doing neck surgery is best. The results aren't very strong, so we can't rely on them to know which way is better. The studies also didn't measure how well people felt after the surgery, so we don't know if one type of surgery makes people feel better or worse.

This study looked at two medicines, carbamazepine and topiramate, to see which might help people with a type of seizure called focal onset seizures. Out of the people who took part, about 93% had information on their seizures. Some people in the study had seizures that weren't clearly classified.

The study found that carbamazepine might help people keep their seizures under control longer than topiramate. It also seemed to help people get better faster. But topiramate might be better at helping people stop having seizures right away.

The study showed that carbamazepine might make it less likely for people to stop taking their medicine early. Also, people taking carbamazepine might reach a state where they don't have seizures for a full year sooner than those taking topiramate.

However, the study wasn't perfect. One of the bigger studies might have had some problems because it wasn't double-blinded. This means the doctors knew which medicine people were getting, which could have affected the results.

Overall, the evidence for carbamazepine being better is strong, especially for people with focal seizures. But for people with generalised seizures or seizures that aren't clearly defined, the evidence isn't as strong. More research is needed to confirm these findings.

The study found that the most common side effects were feeling sleepy, tingling sensations, headaches, upset stomachs, and feelings of worry or sadness. These side effects were about the same for both medicines.

The researchers think that future studies should be done carefully to make sure they're fair and accurate. They suggest making sure the studies are double-blinded, choosing the right group of people to study, using clear definitions for different types of seizures, and looking at long enough to see if the medicines work.

output:
In a review of 33 studies, researchers looked at different ways to encourage people to be more active in their communities. They studied 267 communities, which ranged from small places with less than 500 people to larger areas with over 1.9 million people. Most of the studies came from richer countries, but some were done in poorer countries too.

The studies tried different things like working with local government and non-profit groups. But none of them looked at whether these programs helped people who didn't have much money or lived in tough neighborhoods. Many of the studies weren't very good because they might have picked communities that would work well for their program.

Out of the studies that did try to help people be more active, most didn't show that it worked. Only a few studies that were done better showed that people walked more in the area where the program was. But even these studies didn't show that overall, people became more active.

Some studies said that fewer people were inactive after the program started, but this wasn't true for everyone in the community. Also, the studies that were done best didn't find that people became more active either.

The studies also didn't tell us if the programs cost too much money or if they could keep working long-term. There wasn't enough information about costs and how long the programs lasted.

Overall, the studies didn't find that big programs to make communities more active really work. But some programs that focused on making changes in the environment, like improving sidewalks or working with police, seemed to get more people walking. However, we don't know if these changes made people more active in the long run.

output:
This study looked at a medicine called L-ornithine L-aspartate to see if it helps people with liver problems. They checked 36 studies that involved more than 2300 people. But they could only use information from 29 studies with 1891 people. 

The medicine seemed to help lower the chance of dying (mortality) compared to nothing or other medicines. But this wasn't always true when they only looked at the studies that were done well. The studies also suggested it might help with a condition called hepatic encephalopathy, which makes people act funny or confused. Again, this wasn't always true when they only looked at the best-studied ones.

There was some evidence that taking the medicine might make fewer people get very sick, but this wasn't always clear. The studies weren't very good, so we're not sure if these findings are real. The medicine didn't seem to help with other problems like feeling better overall or having side effects.

When comparing it to other medicines, the medicine didn't seem to help much. It didn't seem to help with dying, being confused, or getting sick. But it did seem to help a little bit with being confused, especially when compared to another medicine called probiotics.

More studies are needed to confirm these findings, especially studies that haven't been published yet.

output:
This study looked at two medicines, phenytoin and sodium valproate, to see which might help stop seizures better. They studied 11 different groups of people who had seizures. Out of the people they studied, only about 60% had full information about their results.

The study found that it might take longer for the medicine to stop working completely (called "treatment failure") if someone takes phenytoin compared to sodium valproate. But it's not very clear if this happens because the medicine isn't working well or because of side effects like feeling sleepy or having a rash.

For when a person has their first seizure again after starting the medicine, it seems like it might happen sooner with sodium valproate than with phenytoin. But again, this isn't very clear.

The study also found that it might take longer for the medicine to work really well (called "remission") if someone takes phenytoin compared to sodium valproate. But this isn't very clear either.

There wasn't much information about whether one medicine causes more side effects than the other. Both medicines can cause side effects like feeling tired, having a rash, or feeling dizzy.

Most of the studies used a type of design where doctors knew which medicine people were taking, which might make the results less reliable. Also, some of the studies didn't always clearly say what kind of seizure someone had, which might have made the results confusing.

Overall, the study couldn't tell us for sure if one medicine works better than the other for stopping seizures. It suggests that maybe sodium valproate might work a little bit better, but it's not very clear. The study also says that future studies should be done carefully to get clearer answers.

This research looked at different treatments for a condition called diabetic retinopathy (PDR) in 1005 people. The studies were mostly done in Asia, Europe, the Middle East, North America, and South America. Some studies gave people a treatment called bevacizumab along with another treatment called PRP, while others just gave PRP. Other studies gave people a treatment called anti-VEGF, which includes bevacizumab, pegaptanib, or ranibizumab. 

The studies lasted from 1 to 12 months. Most of the studies had some problems that made the results less reliable. One study found that people who got bevacizumab and PRP were less likely to lose their vision than those who only got PRP. Another study found that people who got anti-VEGF were more likely to get back some of their vision. But the results weren't always clear.

People who got anti-VEGF had better vision after 12 months compared to those who didn't get it. They also had fewer problems like bleeding inside the eye. However, the results for bevacizumab weren't as clear. Bevacizumab helped prevent losing vision, but it wasn't always clear if it helped people see better.

Overall, the evidence suggests that anti-VEGF treatments can help reduce bleeding in the eye, but we need more studies to be sure. The results are not very strong because many of the studies had problems and the effects weren't always consistent. More research will help us understand these treatments better.

The study lasted for 6 to 24 months.

The results showed that people taking fingolimod were more likely to stay healthy and not have their condition get worse over time. This happened especially with the lower dose of fingolimod. But, there wasn't much difference between those taking fingolimod and those taking a different medicine called intramuscular interferon beta-1a.

Fingolimod also seemed to help reduce inflammation in the brain, which is good. However, people taking higher doses of fingolimod were more likely to stop taking the medicine because of side effects. Also, people taking fingolimod were more likely to stop taking the medicine because of side effects compared to people taking other medicines for MS.

Overall, fingolimod seems to be helpful in treating MS, but it's important to watch for side effects. More research is needed to fully understand how well it works compared to other medicines.

This research looked at different kinds of artificial lenses (IOLs) used after cataract surgery for people who have a condition called uveitis. They studied four large studies with a total of 216 people. The studies compared different types of IOLs like hydrophobic acrylic, silicone, HSM PMMA, and unmodified PMMA. 

The biggest study had 140 people, and they found that most people got better vision with any of the IOL types. But when comparing hydrophobic acrylic IOLs to silicone IOLs, fewer eyes developed something called posterior synechiae, which is when the iris sticks to the lens. This happened less often with hydrophobic acrylic IOLs. However, the difference wasn't very clear for other problems like PCO (cloudiness in the lens), corneal swelling, or cystoid macular edema (a swelling in the part of the eye that helps you see clearly).

The studies weren't perfect because some didn't hide who was getting which IOL, and not all the people who were supposed to be in the study actually were. Also, the studies were small, so it's hard to know if the results apply to everyone.

Overall, the research suggests that none of the IOL types are clearly better than the others for people with uveitis. More studies are needed to find out which type might work best.

This research looked at 21 studies involving more than a million people in Africa, the Americas, and South-East Asia. These studies tested different kinds of unconditional cash transfers (UCTs), which are like giving money to people without asking them to do anything specific in return. The studies gave out cash worth about 1.3% to 53.9% of each person's yearly earnings.

Most of these studies had some problems, so we're not sure how good they are. But most of the time, the studies showed that UCTs might help people feel better about their health. They found that after about a year, people who got UCTs were less likely to get sick in the past few months. Also, they were more likely to eat a variety of foods and go to school. 

However, we're not sure if UCTs make a big difference in other areas like how much money people spend on health care, how well people are doing financially, or how well parents are taking care of their kids. There wasn't enough information to know if UCTs cause any bad effects. Some studies showed that UCTs might help people stay in school longer, but we're not sure if this happens everywhere. Overall, while UCTs seem to help with some things, we don't know if they work better than another kind of program called conditional cash transfers (CCTs).

This research looked at different ways to help stop elder abuse. They found seven studies that involved 1924 older adults and 740 others. These studies tried different things like special programs, rules about elder abuse, and laws against it. But they didn't find studies about specific educational programs or policies.

All the studies had a control group, meaning some people got the treatment and others did not. Most of the studies said they picked who got the treatment fairly. But only one study was very good at picking who got the treatment, and two studies had some problems.

The studies were mostly done in rich countries. None told us if the programs helped everyone equally. Some studies showed the programs might make caregivers feel less anxious and depressed. But other studies showed mixed results, sometimes saying the programs worked and sometimes not.

It's hard to know if these programs really work because the studies weren't always done well. We don't have enough good information to say for sure if these programs prevent or stop elder abuse. More studies are needed, especially from poorer countries, to see if these programs actually help. And all future studies should look at how much money these programs cost and if they work for everyone.

output: This research looked at 681 people and kids who had their asthma get worse. The studies were done on different ages and some didn't include people who might need antibiotics right away. Some used antibiotics like macrolides and others used penicillin, which is older medicine. Five studies compared taking antibiotics to not taking them. They found that people who took antibiotics had slightly fewer asthma symptoms and could breathe better after 10 days. But the studies weren't perfect, so we're not sure if this really works. There wasn't enough information about other important things like whether people got sicker or if they stayed in the hospital. Overall, the results aren't very strong because the studies were different and some were done a long time ago. So we can't be totally sure if antibiotics help with asthma, but they seem to help a little bit.

This research looked at different ways to help people stop smoking before they have surgery. They studied thirteen trials with 2,010 people. Some of the trials didn't tell us if stopping smoking happened, but most did. The studies were mostly done well, but there weren't many of them, so we're not very sure about the results.

Ten out of the thirteen trials looked at helping people stop smoking right before their surgery. Eight of those trials gave some kind of nicotine replacement therapy (like patches or gum) to the people. Two trials gave extra help right before the surgery, like having lots of talks with a counselor. One trial gave extra help to both groups, plus a computer program to help them quit smoking. One trial looked at giving a medicine called varenicline just before the surgery and another looked at giving nicotine lozenges (like little candies with nicotine) the night before.

The results showed that people who got extra help were more likely to stop smoking right before their surgery compared to those who didn't get extra help. This extra help also seemed to help prevent problems after the surgery. But the medicine varenicline didn't seem to help people stop smoking right before their surgery, though it might help them stop later.

For preventing problems after the surgery, the extra help worked better. People who got extra help were less likely to have problems after the surgery. But the extra help didn't seem to work as well for helping people stop smoking right before the surgery.

One trial of varenicline showed that it helped people stop smoking later, but it didn't help them stop right before the surgery or prevent problems after the surgery.

So, it seems that giving extra help to people before their surgery can help them stop smoking and prevent problems after the surgery. But we need more research to know exactly how much help works best and when it should start.

This review looked at 10 studies to see if certain treatments could help prevent white spots called dental lesions (DLs) on teeth during orthodontic treatment. Out of these studies, some had better methods to avoid mistakes in their results, while others did not. 

Two studies showed that using a special foam with a lot of fluoride (12,300 parts per million) applied by a dentist every two months might help prevent DLs. Another study found that using a very strong fluoride toothpaste (5000 parts per million) instead of a regular one might also work. But other studies didn't find a clear difference between different fluoride treatments.

The studies couldn't prove that any of these treatments worked better than others, so we're not sure yet which one is the best. More studies are needed to be really confident about which treatment works best. Also, it's important to know if people actually use the fluoride treatments as recommended and if there are any side effects. Future studies should follow patients after their orthodontic treatment to see if the treatments improve their satisfaction with the treatment.

In a study looking at different ways to treat tooth problems, researchers looked at 20 studies. Some studies compared getting a small part of the tooth removed and filling it with special material to just cleaning out the problem area. Other studies looked at different ways to see inside the tooth before treatment, different tools to see better during treatment, different ways to make the hole in the tooth, different materials to fill the hole, and whether using lasers helped heal the tooth.

The studies didn't find strong proof that one way was better than another for making the tooth healthy again after a year. But they did find that people who had the tooth worked on had more pain in the first week after treatment compared to those who just cleaned the tooth.

Some studies suggested that using a special material called MTA might help the tooth heal better than just cleaning it out. Using a tool called an ultrasonic device to clean the tooth might also help it heal faster.

However, there wasn't enough good evidence to show that using X-rays instead of other kinds of pictures before treatment helps heal the tooth better. Also, using different tools to see inside the tooth didn't seem to make much difference.

There wasn't enough proof to show that taking a special medicine before the treatment helps prevent infections. But using a special gel that helps new tissue grow back after the treatment seemed to help reduce pain afterward.

Using a laser to treat the tooth didn't seem to help with pain either. Overall, the studies didn't give doctors clear advice on the best way to treat tooth problems. More research is needed to figure out the best treatments and how they affect how well teeth feel after being treated. Future studies should use the same methods and measure the same things to get better answers.

In a study looking at different ways to help people who might get a mental illness called psychosis, researchers looked at 20 studies with 2151 people. They compared different treatments like amino acids, omega-3 fatty acids, and some types of therapy. One thing they looked at was if these treatments helped stop people from getting psychosis.

For omega-3 fatty acids, they found that fewer people in the group taking omega-3s got psychosis compared to those taking a placebo over a long time (seven years). But for other treatments like amisulpiride, olanzapine, and some types of therapy, they didn't find any clear difference in stopping people from getting psychosis.

The evidence wasn't very strong for most of these comparisons. It's like when you're trying to decide which ice cream flavor is better - sometimes it's hard to tell because the flavors aren't very different. So while omega-3 fatty acids seemed to work a little bit, we need more research to know for sure. Other treatments didn't seem to make much difference either. More studies are needed to learn more about what helps prevent people from getting psychosis.

output: This study looked at 35 trials that tested if eating cocoa products helps lower blood pressure. In these trials, people took cocoa products with 30 to 1218 milligrams of something called flavanols every day. The control group, who didn't get cocoa, had cocoa products with less flavanols or none at all. After looking at all the data, they found that people who ate cocoa products with more flavanols had slightly lower blood pressure than those who didn't eat cocoa. This happened mostly in people with normal blood pressure, but it wasn't clear if it helped people with higher blood pressure. The study suggests that cocoa might help lower blood pressure, but more research is needed to confirm this. The results are not very strong because the studies weren't exactly the same. Eating cocoa was generally safe, but some people had stomach problems. More long-term studies are needed to see if cocoa affects heart health over time.

output: A study looked at 77 trials involving 40,249 women and their babies. Most of the trials had lots of participants, and all but one of those big ones happened in countries where people have more money. The study found that taking a little medicine called low-dose aspirin helped prevent some problems during pregnancy. It lowered the chance of a condition called proteinuric pre-eclampsia by about 18%, which means one out of every 61 women who took the medicine didn't get this condition. It also slightly lowered the chances of having a baby born too early or too small, and it helped reduce the risk of the baby dying. However, it might make it a tiny bit harder for the woman to lose her blood after giving birth. The study found that giving aspirin to 1000 women could help avoid about 20 more serious problems during pregnancy. All of the information in the study is very reliable. More research is needed to see if giving higher doses of aspirin works better and if it's safe to start giving it earlier in pregnancy.

output: This study looked at different ways to help people avoid getting a sickness called AMS when they go to high altitudes. They checked 20 studies with 1406 people to see if certain things worked. For some methods like using air pressure machines or special breathing exercises, it's not clear if they help prevent AMS. The evidence isn't strong because there weren't many studies. Some supplements like antioxidants, iron, and a plant called Rhodiola might not help, but again, we're not sure. Erythropoietin, which is a medicine, seems to help a bit, but the evidence isn't very good. Ginkgo biloba, another supplement, didn't show much effect in most studies, but combining it with another medicine called acetazolamide seemed to work better. There wasn't enough information about whether these methods cause problems. This review is part of a bigger set of studies trying to find out the best ways to prevent AMS. The evidence isn't very strong, and more studies are needed to know if these methods really work or if they have side effects.

This research looked at 54 studies about exercise for people with knee osteoarthritis (OA). Out of these, 19 studies had good ways to make sure they were fair and didn't miss any information. Most studies were done well, but some might have been influenced by who knew what kind of exercise they were getting.

The studies found that exercise helped reduce pain right away. People who didn't get exercise had pain that was like 44 out of 100, but those who exercised felt less pain, like 32 out of 100. Exercise also helped them move better and feel better overall. Their quality of life went up too, like going from 43 out of 100 to 47 out of 100.

Exercise didn't cause many problems, but sometimes it made their knees or backs hurt more. Most studies lasted for two to six months, and during that time, people who exercised still felt better than those who didn't.

The studies showed that exercise worked well for knee pain and helped people move better. But the effects weren't huge—like a little bit better, but not super noticeable. It's hard to know if the improvements were just because people knew they were exercising or if it really helped. Still, the benefits seemed pretty clear. More research might show different results, but we think the current findings are reliable.

This research looked at whether teaching health professionals about cultural differences helps patients from different backgrounds get better care. They studied five groups of healthcare workers and over 8,000 patients. Most of the patients were from cultures different from the healthcare workers. The studies compared two things: teaching health workers about cultural differences and not teaching them. 

The studies found that teaching didn't seem to help patients reach their cholesterol goals or lose more weight. But it did make patients feel like they understood their doctors better. Also, patients who saw doctors from different backgrounds said they felt more comfortable and understood.

Some studies found that patients were happier with their doctor visits after the training. But other studies didn't find this. Overall, the studies weren't very strong because they had many differences in how they were done. We need more research to know if teaching cultural skills really helps patients.

The research team made a plan to help everyone agree on how to describe and measure these kinds of training programs. They think future studies should look at how well these programs work in real-world settings and see if they help hospitals use the training.

This research looked at 12 studies with 1554 people to see if taking special good bacteria called probiotics could help prevent and treat diarrhea caused by radiation therapy or chemotherapy. The studies had different ways they were done, so it's hard to compare them directly. 

For preventing radiation therapy-induced diarrhea, the studies showed that probiotics might slightly lower the chance of getting diarrhea, but the evidence isn't very strong. They also didn't find clear benefits for quality of life. For more severe diarrhea (grade 2 or higher), the studies weren't able to show if probiotics helped or not. 

When it came to treating diarrhea, some studies suggested probiotics might help reduce the need for medicine to stop the diarrhea, but again, the evidence wasn't very strong. There were no big problems like death or serious side effects in these studies.

Overall, the research suggests that probiotics might help a little bit, but we need more studies to be sure. The current evidence is not very strong because the studies were small and didn't always agree with each other. Future studies should be bigger and better designed to give us clearer answers.

This study looked at five trials involving 368 people with pain in their kneecaps when they exercised. The people in the studies were mostly from health clinics or were new soldiers going through training. None of the trials involved elite athletes. All the trials had some problems keeping things fair, like making sure neither the doctors nor the patients knew which treatment was being used. The information isn't very reliable because it's hard to be sure if the results are true.

The trials compared different types of knee braces or straps to see if they helped with knee pain. They didn't find that any of the knee braces or straps worked better than just doing exercises. Some people got a little bit less pain, but it wasn't enough to really notice. They also didn't find that any of the knee braces or straps made knee function better.

None of the trials looked at how well people could play sports or work after getting the knee braces or straps. Only one trial mentioned that some people stopped training because of knee pain, but it wasn't clear if this happened more often with the knee braces or straps.

Overall, the studies didn't show that knee braces or straps help with knee pain in people who are exercising. More research is needed to know if these knee braces and straps are helpful for treating knee pain while someone is exercising.

This study looked at 183 studies involving 252,886 people. Many of the studies used a type of antibiotic called macrolides. These antibiotics were used to treat or prevent things like colds, heart problems, breathing issues, stomach problems, and other health concerns. Most of the studies happened in hospitals.

The studies showed that people taking macrolides had more digestive problems like diarrhea, stomach pain, and feeling sick to their stomach compared to those taking a sugar pill. For every 1,000 people taking macrolides, about 85 more people had digestive problems, 72 more had stomach pain, 47 more felt sick to their stomach, and 23 more threw up. It's like saying if you give 17 people macrolides, one of them might have more stomach pain.

There were also more taste problems when people took macrolides. But it wasn't clear if this was a real problem or just because people thought it was happening. Taking macrolides didn't seem to cause more hearing problems, heart problems, liver problems, or make people lose their appetite. They also didn't find more skin problems or rashes.

Macrolides seemed to help people cough less and have fewer colds compared to a sugar pill. They also didn't seem to cause more deaths. However, it's hard to know if macrolides caused more resistance to the antibiotics themselves, which means the bacteria might be harder to treat later.

Most of the studies didn't do a good job of listing all the possible side effects or how they found out about them. Some studies got money from the companies that make the medicine. Overall, macrolides caused more digestive problems, but the evidence isn't perfect.

This review looked at five studies involving 71,458 women to see if counting fetal movements helps during pregnancy. Most of these studies weren't very good at showing they didn't have problems. They mostly studied women who had normal pregnancies.

Two studies compared counting fetal movements to regular care. One found that women who counted movements had less anxiety, but there wasn't much difference in how many babies died or had serious health problems. Another study found that more women in the counting group went to the hospital early, but there was no clear difference in how many babies had low birth weights.

One big study found that women who counted their baby's movements more often had fewer cesarean sections. But there was no clear difference in how many babies died or had serious health problems.

Another study compared two ways of counting fetal movements. Women who counted once a day had fewer hospital visits, but women who counted more often had slightly better scores for their babies right after birth.

The evidence isn't very strong because the studies were small and didn't always do things the same way. Also, it's hard to know if the counting helped because the studies didn't compare it to not doing anything.

Overall, the review doesn't give enough information to change how doctors usually take care of pregnant women. More research is needed to see if counting fetal movements really helps, especially when there might be a problem with the baby.

This review looked at 24 studies involving 10,056 women. Most of the studies came from countries like the USA, UK, Canada, and Australia. The studies compared different ways of teaching new mothers how to breastfeed their babies. They didn't find much difference between the groups when it came to how long a baby was breastfed, whether the baby was getting only breast milk, or if the mother started breastfeeding right away. Some studies showed that teaching might help a little bit, but the results weren't very clear. There wasn't enough information about how breastfeeding problems like sore nipples happened. The studies also didn't show that teaching helped start breastfeeding better. 

When they combined the results of some studies, they found that teaching might make it a tiny bit more likely that a baby would be fed only breast milk for three months, but the results weren't very strong. Teaching didn't seem to affect how often a baby was fed breast milk overall or how long the baby was breastfed. 

The review couldn't tell us if teaching worked better for mothers who had higher or lower levels of education. They also couldn't do a special look at mothers who worked or didn't work outside the home. Overall, the studies didn't show that teaching before a baby is born helps start or continue breastfeeding. More research is needed to see if teaching works well and if it has any bad side effects, especially in places where people don't have lots of money.

In a study looking at different treatments for shoulder problems called rotator cuff disease, researchers looked at 60 trials involving 3,620 people. They found that one trial compared getting manual therapy (special touch treatments), exercise, and inactive ultrasound (placebo) to just inactive ultrasound. This trial involved 120 people who had shoulder pain for a long time.

At the end of 22 weeks, the group that got manual therapy and exercise had less pain and better shoulder movement compared to the group that only got inactive ultrasound. More people in the manual therapy and exercise group said their shoulder felt better, but there were also more people who had some short-term pain after the treatment.

However, other studies didn't find much difference between manual therapy and exercise and other treatments like shots of medicine, surgery, or special exercises. Some studies even suggested that manual therapy and exercise might not work as well as acupuncture and a special supplement.

The evidence about whether manual therapy and exercise help more than taking pain medicine or if adding shots to the treatment helps more wasn't very strong, so we're not sure about that.

Most of the studies about manual therapy or exercise alone weren't very good quality, so we don't know if they really make a big difference. Sometimes, doing exercise alone helped a bit less with pain, but not with how well you could move your shoulder.

When comparing manual therapy and exercise to other treatments, there wasn't much difference in how well people did. The treatments caused a bit more side effects, but these were usually minor.

Future studies should compare manual therapy and exercise to something that looks similar but doesn't actually work, to see if that makes a difference. And more studies are needed to see if these treatments work better than other options for rotator cuff problems.

output: This review looked at seven studies, including five done in children and two in adults. Most of the studies were done well, but one in adults wasn't done as well and didn't give us all the information we needed. For children, who have really bad sore throats, having their tonsils and adenoids removed helps them have fewer sore throats overall. They had about 3.6 sore throats in the first year after the surgery, compared to 3.6 sore throats in the group that didn't have the surgery. But for kids who already had pretty bad sore throats, the surgery helped a little bit by reducing their sore throats by about one episode. For kids who didn't have such bad sore throats, the surgery actually made their sore throats worse. In the first year after the surgery, children who had the procedure had about 18 days of sore throats, while those who didn't have the surgery had about 23 days. For adults, having the surgery within six months after the procedure led to about 3.6 fewer sore throat episodes, but the results weren't very strong because the studies were different from each other. The surgery also seemed to make sore throats go away faster. There's not enough information to know if the surgery works better or worse for adults. The surgery does help reduce sore throats in children, but the effect is very small. The surgery might help predict when one sore throat episode will happen right after the surgery. But the surgery isn't perfect—it can cause bleeding and is uncomfortable for adults. Overall, the surgery seems to help a little bit, but the benefits are small and need to be balanced against the risks.

output: This review looked at studies about whether giving antibiotics later instead of right away helps when someone has a sickness like a sore throat or ear infection. They checked if waiting to give antibiotics made a difference in how sick people felt, if they got better faster, or if their bodies had fewer problems. They found that for some sicknesses, like sore throats and ear infections, waiting to give antibiotics didn't make people feel worse or get better slower. It also helped people use fewer antibiotics overall. This means that sometimes, if a doctor thinks it's okay, they might wait to give antibiotics instead of giving them right away. This could help stop bacteria from becoming resistant to antibiotics, which is important because it makes it harder to treat infections. But it's still important to follow the doctor's advice and go back if the symptoms don't go away. The studies showed that waiting to give antibiotics wasn't different from not giving any antibiotics at all in terms of making people feel better or having fewer problems.
